source.title: Structuring Sparsity: Block-Sparse Featurizers Capture Visual Concept Manifolds
source.authors: Thomas Fel; M. Kowal; Mozes Jacobs; Dron Hazra; Usha Bhalla; Lee Sharkey; Lucius Bushnaq; Satchel Grant; Tal Haklay; Thomas Icard; Can Rager; Michael T. Pearce; Daniel Wurgaft; Aiden Swann; Fenil R. Doshi; S. Boppana; Curt Tigges; Nick Cammarata; Thomas Serre; V. Shyam; Owen Lewis; Tom McGrath; Jack Merullo; E. Lubana; Atticus Geiger

page_placements.theme: Multi-dimensional (circular or manifold) features are fragmented by unit-level analyses

record.tranche_reason: The paper reinterprets InceptionV1 curve-detector responses as readings from a shared continuous curve manifold, refining how this visual representation should be described.
record.gate_note: The paper measures a Grassmannian BSF block over synthetic curve orientations and reports its coverage and Fourier structure, including matched nulls. The neuron and Top-K SAE tuning curves shown for comparison are attributed to Cammarata et al. (2020) and Gorton (2024), so those cited results are not recorded as rows. It does not test responses to unrelated input categories or the prevalence of polysemantic neurons.
record.test_reason: The study shows that InceptionV1 curve-detector neurons and SAE atoms each cover a narrow orientation wedge, and that one BSF block recovers the whole orientation manifold. Curve detectors are not polysemantic: no neuron here responds to unrelated inputs. The finding concerns one feature spread across many neurons, not one neuron carrying several features. So it does not bear on V6, which is about canonical mixed-concept neurons such as cat/car turning out to share one feature. No other version is tested: no prevalence counts, no language models, no causal test of capacity pressure, and no architecture comparisons of polysemantic share. The toy 'manifold superposition' experiment scores featurizer recovery, not neuron polysemanticity.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct for the InceptionV1 section. The authors conclude that curve-detector neurons and SAE atoms give a fractured view of one continuous curve manifold. They say the SAE tiling is an artifact of a mismatched directional prior, not a property of the network. A single BSF block recovers the manifold, and its 2nd and 3rd harmonics are real and explain 180°-wrapping curve neurons. The paper's broader conclusions: block sparsity is the matched prior for a sparse sum of manifolds; BSFs describe DINOv3 activations more compactly than SAEs, with concepts about 2–4 dimensional; BSFs find lighting and shadow manifolds in DINOv3; and they support manifold steering in SDXL.
record.recipe_differences: Uses block-sparse featurizers and Fourier analysis of InceptionV1 curve responses, rather than the neuron-level circuit analysis or SoLU method named in the original sources.

fits_no_version.finding: InceptionV1 curve-detector neurons and Top-K SAE atoms each tile a narrow orientation wedge. A single Grassmannian BSF block is active at all orientations and carries the orientation circle plus significant 2nd and 3rd Fourier harmonics: 18.3% and 12.0% of AC variance, far above a matched null. Some neurons' 180° wrapping matches the 2nd harmonic.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Families of monosemantic-looking neurons or SAE atoms can be fragmented readings of one continuous low-dimensional feature manifold.

record.problems: The curve-manifold analysis is a narrow case and does not assess unrelated input mixtures or the prevalence of polysemantic neurons. The neuron and SAE comparisons are cited from prior work rather than newly measured here.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible results omitted. Cited neuron and Top-K SAE tuning results in Section 4 and Figure 11 were not entered as rows because they are results from prior work.

untested.parts: No test of single neurons responding to unrelated inputs in vision models.
Toy manifold-superposition data test featurizer recovery, not whether capacity pressure causes neuron polysemanticity.
No test of initialization, regularization or noise as causes.
No measure of polysemantic neuron share across architectures or training choices.
Curve detectors are not canonical polysemantic neurons. No mixed-concept neuron is reinterpreted, and the rarity of unrelated mixtures is not assessed.
No comparison of polysemanticity judgments across activation ranges or scoring methods.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the curve analysis to V6, but curve detectors are the canonical monosemantic example, not polysemantic neurons. The paper never measures neurons responding to unrelated inputs. The neuron and SAE tuning curves in Fig. 11a are cited from Cammarata et al. (2020) and Gorton (2024). Coverage 1.0 comes from Appendix E.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether individual neurons respond to several unrelated input kinds.
No language models or token/context polysemanticity are tested.
The toy experiment tests recovery of additive manifold factors, not whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by capacity pressure.
Does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemantic neurons.
Compares featurizers and block dimensions, but does not measure how architecture or training changes the share of polysemantic neurons or its performance cost.

Tests the interpretation of the InceptionV1 curve-detector representation, not canonical mixed-concept neurons such as 4e:55, the frequency of truly unrelated mixtures, or whether unrelated mixtures are generally rare.
Does not compare polysemanticity judgments across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Swept synthetic curve orientation and measured coverage of one Grassmannian BSF block.
rows.measure: Orientation coverage of the recovered curve-manifold block
rows.note: The authors describe the single block as reconstructing the whole curve manifold as one connected region.
rows.check: Orientation coverage of a featurizer block measures manifold recovery, not whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Curve detectors are not polysemantic, so this does not bear on V6.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4 (single Grassmannian BSF block active across all orientations, b=16); Appendix E: coverage 1.0

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Decomposed the recovered block contribution during an orientation sweep into Fourier harmonics.
rows.measure: Share of AC variance by Fourier mode
rows.value: recovered manifold: k=1 58.9%, k=2 18.3%, k=3 12.0%, k=4 7.2%
rows.uncertainty: The text reports 18.3% and 12.0% exceed the matched-noise null by factors of 470 and 314; z ≈ 1.5 × 10^3 and 9 × 10^2 over 200 draws.
rows.note: The first three modes account for 89% in the rounded main-text report; the table gives the more precise percentages recorded here.
rows.check: Fourier mode shares of the BSF block's orientation response describe how one feature is encoded. They do not measure neuron polysemanticity or a reinterpretation of mixed-concept neurons.

relation.reason: It revisits curve-detector neurons (Cammarata et al. 2020; Olah et al. 2020) as a testbed and reinterprets 180°-wrapping curve neurons. It does not test whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs.

tranche.reason: The paper tests whether block-sparse featurizers recover manifolds, using InceptionV1 curve detectors as a known case. Curve detectors are not polysemantic, and the paper never mentions polysemanticity, so no version is tested.

source_check.notes: All 5 rows match Appendix E Table 1 and Section 4. No verdicts, which is right. Shares authors with an original (Cammarata). Minor: the text gives the white-noise floor as 0.06% per mode, while Table 1 shows 0.04% for the matched-noise null.
